html:
I lived in Germany for four years.

  1. Boredom is a required course. A PhD is a grind in itself, and when I first arrived in Germany, all I could say was guten Tag, mein Name ist (hello, my name is), so I often found myself wondering where I was and what I was doing there. As my German improved, I gradually got used to research life and the local ways, made some friends, and the boredom eased. But don’t get me wrong: it still doesn’t compare with life in China. Working there may mean overtime, a fast pace and lots of pressure, but damn, the entertainment is rich.
  2. Language. As I’ve griped in some other answers, “Sie sind in Deutschland. Sie müssen Deutsch lernen!” (You’re in Germany. You must learn German!) is a jab your surroundings give you all the time. You can survive in Germany with English alone, but survive is about all you’ll do. Germans have an innate pride in their mother tongue and feel that German is the true world language. No wonder they think so: Germany is a big country by European standards (believe me, in Europe it really is big, even though it’s only three quarters the size of Heilongjiang province), and German is spoken not just in Germany but also in Austria, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, Namibia and Mallorca in Spain (I’m making the last two up). Within Europe, more countries use it than use English. Add an economy that has been strong for years, and a quiet little pride lurking behind a dark history they’re ashamed to mention, and they can’t help feeling like a great nation second to none. Don’t expect the auntie at the supermarket checkout to switch to English for you, even if she understands it perfectly and can speak it too. Here’s a little trick that has never failed me. When you deal with some office, say the town hall, if you start in German and then stumble or say something unidiomatic, the person across the desk can easily turn arrogant. But if you prepare all your questions in English beforehand and, without even asking Können wir auf Englisch sprechen (can we talk in English), just launch straight into English, they tend to be friendly, even a little humble and guilty. Perfectionism isn’t a purely German trait; when it comes to languages, it applies to every people. That said, if you want to live more comfortably and happily in Germany and try to understand and fit into the country, German is a must. German research and industry are so strong that even if you work or study in another country, you’ll still end up dealing with Germany from time to time. My company often does business with German companies or goes to conferences and trade fairs in Germany, and that’s when speaking German really pays off, because some Germans genuinely won’t speak a word of English.
  3. Culture. Sorry, but if you came to Germany after the age of fifteen, it’s really hard to fit in culturally, even once language is no longer a barrier. When we bring up the Calabash Brothers cartoon, the Monkey King, Lady White Snake and Jin Yong’s Demi-Gods and Semi-Devils, or ration coupons, the Cultural Revolution, the Young Pioneers, flag-raising every Monday and school uniforms, someone will suddenly pipe up: “Sorry, I don’t think I understood that” (in a Siri voice). Without growing up together, you can’t share that kind of resonance. And it’s not just Germany: the whole of Western society, plus the Americas, shares a common cultural background, a bit like the different provinces of China, which have their own dialects but where everyone instantly gets all the things I listed above. Of course, you can try to make up for it: cram their music, films and history, and live through their childhood all over again. But values are something you just can’t change.
  4. Seeing a doctor: a pain in the ass. First you go to a Hausarzt, a family doctor, who decides based on your condition whether to refer you; then, with a referral slip (Überweisung), you go to the hospital to see a specialist. The whole process is painfully slow. In just four years I went through a sprained ankle, a tooth extraction, an allergy, a fever, a broken bone, a shard of glass in my finger and more. With the sprained ankle I waited five hours in the ER; after the tooth extraction I got no painkillers; for the fever I was prescribed antibiotics without being asked about allergies, which gave me an allergic reaction (by the way, that time the ER did see me quickly). Overall, the doctors lacked experience and weren’t very dedicated; usually only fairly serious problems got their attention. My wife once had a minor operation; the staff were very kind, the hospital was well equipped, and her stay was quiet and restful, unlike hospitals in China, where you always feel tense and stressed. Still, everything is relative: since moving to the Netherlands, I’ve found it’s even worse here. Getting your Hausarzt to write an Überweisung takes strong dialectical reasoning and real acting skills.
  5. Housing: moving out is a battle. I’ve seen a friend’s German landlord come in for the move-out inspection wearing a Hermès belt and, in under a second, point out ten things that weren’t OK, plainly out to squeeze money out of him. My place was run by a property management company, so I didn’t deal with a landlord, but that didn’t stop the people I did deal with from being bitchy. When I found the apartment and signed the lease, I met them a few times, and the woman from the company looked at me as if I were a spy; when I made small talk with her, she asked, “What is the reason behind your question?” Moving out was even more of a drama: they picked out endless faults, and every word was full of distrust and contempt. When I suggested they could make an English version of the lease, she shouted the famous line that speaks for every German heart:

“Sie sind in Deutschland. Sie müssen Deutsch lernen!!!”

Even though I’d been speaking German to her the whole time.


Frustrations aside, Germany’s advantages are obvious too: a strong economy, lots of jobs, high salaries and low prices. If the frustrations above don’t count as frustrations for you, Germany is an excellent choice.
